title: Illusion of Skill
hook: A rising tide can make every rower in the boat look brilliant.
counterintuition: Good results may belong to the current, not the captain; test skill against conditions before rewarding or copying it.
tryThisNow: Pick one success you are praising. Write the strongest outside condition that helped it. Then name what skill still remains.
keyTakeaway: The illusion of skill turns favorable conditions into personal credit. Compare results with the wind, base rate, and counterfactual.

breakdown.fastRead: The permit folder in the municipal court lunch calendar shows fewer late returns after Darlene changed the schedule. She wants to credit the clerk who proposed it. But the same month also had fewer hearings and a new online reminder. She writes illusion of skill on the folder, compares similar weeks, and changes the praise to match what the clerk actually controlled.
breakdown.deepRead:
Skill is real. Some people notice more, practice better, and make cleaner choices. The illusion of skill starts when a good outcome is credited to skill before the conditions around it are checked.

A result can ride a current. A hospice letter may raise more donations because a local story made donors ready to give. A college add-drop policy may look smart because enrollment was already shifting. A bakery test may sell out because the weather put more people on the street. The person in charge may still have done good work, but the result is not clean proof.

The current can wear a medal.

The correction is to ask what else moved with the result. What was the market wind? What was the base rate? What happened to comparable teams, stores, courts, or campaigns? What would you expect if the person had done nothing different? A visible check turns praise into evidence.

This matters because false skill credit spreads bad lessons. You copy the wrong manager, reward the wrong tactic, or blame the wrong person when the tide turns. A good review separates what the person controlled from what the setting supplied.
breakdown.fullRead:
The inventory scan in the hospice donation letter review shows a jump in gifts after the new mailing. Terry, the development lead, wants to call the copywriter unusually gifted. The letter may be better. But the same week, a beloved local physician died and the hospice was mentioned in every neighborhood paper. The question is not whether the copy mattered. The question is how much of the lift belonged to the boat.

Warren Buffett's business-boat image is a clean warning. A strong record can come less from heroic rowing than from being in a boat carried by the right business current. Skill still matters, but a favorable current can make ordinary rowing look extraordinary.

What would the result look like in a weaker current?

Kahneman's treatment of skill and luck presses the same point. Where feedback is noisy and conditions move, confidence can grow faster than evidence. People see a streak and infer ability. They see a manager, trader, designer, or coach near success and forget to ask how many others in the same environment rose too.

A ceramics defect pricing review shows the tradeoff. Tove sees a training still from a kiln operator who cut defects during a month of unusually stable clay. The operator may have improved technique. The stable clay may have done half the work. If Tove marks the market wind and compares defect rates across similar clay batches, she can reward the right part. If she praises the whole drop as skill, the next batch will disappoint everyone.

A rower deserves credit for rowing, not for the river.

A ferry terminal passenger sign gives a public example. Zofia watches complaints fall after a new sign is installed. The design team celebrates. Then the budget column shows the same month had fewer sailings, a simpler route mix, and more staff at the gate. The sign may still help. The check is to compare similar traffic days before calling the design brilliant.

The practical correction is a skill audit. First, name the claimed skill. Second, list the external conditions that changed at the same time. Third, compare with a reference group that faced the same conditions. Fourth, ask what result would remain if the wind were removed. Only then should you copy, reward, or scale the tactic.

The limit is that this can become unfair in the other direction. Do not erase skill just because conditions helped. High performers often choose good environments, notice favorable winds, and use them well. The point is not to deny competence. It is to stop treating every good outcome as proof of competence.

Before the choice moves forward, make the boat visible. Put the tide, timing, market, schedule, traffic, or base rate next to the result. If skill remains after that check, trust it more. If it fades, reward the conditions less loudly and keep learning.

examples.title: Darlene separates clerk skill from calendar wind
examples.scenario: A permit folder sits beside the municipal court lunch calendar in Calgary at 12:35 p.m. Darlene must decide whether one clerk's new schedule caused late returns to drop. She marks illusion of skill on the folder, compares similar hearing weeks with and without online reminders, and changes the praise in front of the court administrator.
examples.whatToDo: Compare similar calendar weeks before crediting the clerk's schedule with the full improvement.
examples.whyItMatters: The clerk may have helped, but lighter hearing volume and reminders could also explain the result.

examples.whyItMatters: A good bake can ride a busy noon. The postmortem should separate craft from conditions before scaling the recipe.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Separate skill from conditions before rewarding, copying, or scaling a success.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a result improved, then I will list what changed around the person before assigning credit.
If a test wins, then I will compare it with timing, traffic, and reference groups.
If a bonus depends on better output, then I will check whether inputs or conditions improved too.
If I want to copy a winner, then I will ask whether the winner still wins in a different current.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Pick one recent success. Write the current that helped it and the evidence that skill remains after the current is removed.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, review one result you praised and separate rower, boat, river, and wind.

memorableLines.text: The current can wear a medal.
A rower deserves credit for rowing, not for the river.
Before the choice moves forward, make the boat visible.
